extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent practitioners, and students of patent law (inventors, patent attorneys, judges)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on who is the true inventor and what kinds of inventions/claims are patentable (novelty, public use, utility, combinations, principles carried into practice) under precedents discussed in the treatise. Emphasizes evidentiary and drafting considerations illustrated by cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must have formed the original idea without assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: No person, who has not, without assistance, formed the original idea of the subject in his mind, will be enabled to keep any patent which he may have obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (e.g. Hill v. Thompson). If a person did not originate the idea independently, they cannot be regarded as the inventor entitled to the patent. See also discussion of servants and assistants; the original mental contribution is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assistance from servants — when master or servant is inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: If the servant make a new discovery by himself, such invention becomes his property; but if the master plans, and the servant only executes with alterations of his own, then the master is the true inventor of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Blodam v. Elsee and Donkin's work on the Foudriniers' paper machine: a skilful person employed to assist in completing mechanical contrivances may have those additions belong to the employer who can include them in the specification. Distinguish pure independent discovery by servant (servant's property) from execution of master's plan (master's invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint patentees must be true inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent are often taken out in the joint names of two or three persons. If the secret should be discovered that one or two of those persons bore no part in the invention of the machines, the patents would be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not list persons as joint patentees unless they materially contributed to the invention; inclusion of non-inventors can void the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introducer of a foreign invention / disclosure of foreign source
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention has been obtained from a foreigner, it is common to state in the title that the patentee has received the communication from a person residing abroad, but that fact need not be set forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note legal doubt whether a patent can be supported if the foreign inventor, retaining any interest, is an alien enemy. The text suggests it might be advantageous to permit assignment so an assignee could hold the patent in his own name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture must be new (no prior public use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manufacture must not have been used. The statute (21 Jac. 1, c. 3, s. 6) requires that the manufacture shall be such 'which others, at the time of making such letters patent and grants, shall not use.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of prior use, public operation, or public knowledge can defeat novelty. But mere inaccessible models or incomplete/never-used prototypes shown to a few persons may not be 'public use'. Cases: Lewis v. Alaring, Jones v. Pearce — assessing whether earlier models/specifications amounted to general public use is fact-specific and for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's own public use before application bars patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The true meaning of the words 'not known, or used before the application,' is, not known, or used by the public before the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor makes and sells his invention publicly for years and then seeks a patent, the prior public use by the inventor himself can defeat the later patent (illustrated by Pennock and Sellers v. Dialogue). Courts emphasize that allowing such delay would retard progress and reward secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish public use from experimental/abandoned use
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior use was experimental, not generally known or followed up (abandoned as useless), then a later independent improvement that remedies defects may still be treated as a new invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jones v. Pearce (Strutt's wheels) shows jury must decide whether earlier machines were used openly and continuously (public use) or were mere experiments/abandoned. Experimental trials that are not publicly adopted typically do not defeat later patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture must be material and useful (utility requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manufacture must be material and useful; the question whether a machine is capable of producing useful results is to be decided (e.g. left to the jury in Bloxam v. Elsee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents should be for useful, material inventions; if the device cannot produce the useful result claimed, the patent can fail. Courts will examine the capability and usefulness in fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination or arrangement of known things may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination or arrangement of things already known may be the subject of a grant, provided the particular combination produces a new useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lewis v. Davis: combining a rotatory cutter (old) with modifications to cut from list to list (new arrangement) was held patentable because the combination had not been previously combined. Alterations that are necessary and useful to achieve the new result support patentability; mere aggregation without new effect may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle, method, or process must be carried into practice by tangible means
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle, method, or process must be carried into practice by tangible means; courts construe broad claims to abstract principles as limited to the mechanical means described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial decisions (e.g. construction of Jones's suspension claim) limit claims to the way the principle is 'carried into effect by the mechanical means before described.' Legislative clarity is desirable. Mere statement of a principle without practical means may not be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different patents for same principle allowed if mechanical means differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Several persons may have several patents founded on the same principle, if they use different mechanical contrivances to effect the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hullett v. Hague: same objective (evaporation at low temperature) achieved using the same general idea (heated/forced air) but by different apparatus (perforated coil vs other means) — courts treated the patents as distinct because the means were different. Drafters should claim and describe the specific apparatus/means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting caution — do not claim an unconstrained universal principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a specification's language appears to claim a principle in the abstract, courts may construe it as a claim only to the principle as carried into effect by the described mechanical means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: draft claims to practical embodiments and avoid overbroad language that purports to monopolize an abstract principle; courts will narrow interpretation to described means, and competing inventors may obtain patents for alternative means achieving the same principle.
